## Have the chains converged?

![](images/hairy_caterpillar.jpg){.step}

Straight, plump at both ends, several chains on top of each other.
$\hat{R} = \sqrt{\hat{V}/W}$ compares the variance between chains with the
variance within them. We want this to be below 1.01.

## Before you see the data

![](images/model_checking_prior_predictive.svg){.step}

$\theta^{(i)} \sim p(\theta), \qquad y^{(i)} \sim p(y \mid \theta^{(i)})$

Two hundred draws from our priors. Most burn through the population in a week.

## After fitting

![](images/model_checking_posterior_predictive.svg){.step}

$\theta^{(i)} \sim p(\theta \mid y), \qquad y^{\text{rep},(i)} \sim p(y \mid \theta^{(i)})$

The fit misses both waves: a flatter, later, smaller epidemic that splits the
difference between them.

## Tristan da Cunha, 1971

![](images/TdC.png){.step}

284 people and two waves. [SEITL]{.alert} adds temporary immunity so that a
fraction of those infected return to susceptible — and in a population this
small, chance decides how many.

## Which makes the likelihood an integral

![](images/SEIT4L.jpg){.step}

$$p(\text{data} \mid \theta) = \int_{X} p(\text{data} \mid X, \theta)\, p(X \mid \theta)$$

Run a [stochastic]{.alert} model twice and you get two different trajectories, so
the state $X$ is hidden and random and every path it could have taken counts.
[SEIT4L]{.alert}, with the temporary immunity split four ways, is the version we
fit from here on. That is where today starts.
